I have been farming in Quzhou for over forty years. I never went to school, but I know this land and I watch what the good farmers in my village do. I have about eight mu of good flat land, and every year I grow winter wheat and summer maize — that is the only way to make a living here. 

For the wheat, I will sow in early October after running the rotary tiller to break up the stubble. I use improved wheat seed, about thirty jin per mu, because the old black wheat does not yield enough anymore. I spread compound fertilizer and urea — about eighteen jin of nitrogen, eleven jin of phosphate, and five jin of potash per mu. Wheat is thirsty, so I irrigate three times: once after sowing, once when it greens up in spring, and once at heading. I also spray three times for pests and weeds — mixing insecticide, herbicide, and fungicide together when I can to save labor. If the frost does not hurt it, I expect about one thousand jin per mu, which is five hundred kilograms.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I plant maize without ploughing — just drill the hybrid seed straight into the wheat stubble. I buy the seed by the package, about one package per mu. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat: I give it about twelve jin of nitrogen, four jin of phosphate, and three jin of potash per mu. I irrigate twice, at jointing and grain filling, and spray three times for insects and weeds. In a normal year I can get about one thousand one hundred jin per mu, which is five hundred fifty kilograms. This is what I have always done, and I see no reason to change.
